name: Trend
definition: The general direction in which a security's price is traveling, inferred from the direction of successive peaks and troughs on a chart. Classical technical analysis, following Dow Theory, classifies trends as up, down, or sideways and by duration (primary, secondary, minor); it is an analytical framework for describing price behavior, not a proven predictive law.
intuition: Prices rarely move in straight lines — they zigzag. The trend is simply the direction in which those zigzags lean.
mechanics: Identified from price structure: ascending peaks and troughs indicate an uptrend, descending peaks and troughs a downtrend, and roughly equal peaks and troughs a sideways trend. Analysts commonly visualize trends with trendlines connecting lows or highs, or with moving averages, and classify them by length (primary: ~1 year or more; secondary: weeks to months; minor: under a month).
failure_modes: A trend's turning points are only unambiguous in hindsight, so trend identification always lags; the same security can simultaneously be in an uptrend on one timeframe and a downtrend on another, making the label timeframe-dependent.
misconceptions: That a trend is a force that must continue ('the trend is your friend' taken literally). Apparent trends can arise in random price paths, and trend labels describe the past rather than guarantee the future.
example: A stock rises from 50 to 55, dips to 52, then rises to 58: the ascending peaks (55, 58) and troughs (50, 52) define an uptrend.

name: Uptrend
definition: A trend characterized by a series of ascending peaks and troughs — successively higher highs and higher lows. It is the classical chart-based description of sustained demand exceeding supply; an analytical construct, not evidence that prices must keep rising.
intuition: Each rally carries price further than the last, and each dip stops at a higher floor — a staircase climbing upward.
mechanics: Identified when each successive swing high exceeds the prior swing high and each successive swing low holds above the prior swing low. Often visualized with an up trendline connecting two or more rising lows; the uptrend is conventionally considered intact while price stays above that line or the last higher low.
failure_modes: The structure breaks the moment a lower low prints, but that break is only confirmable after it happens; sharp news-driven declines can invalidate an uptrend without warning.
misconceptions: That every dip in an uptrend is a buying opportunity; any pullback can deepen into a full reversal, and the difference is clear only in retrospect.
example: A stock rises 50 to 55, pulls back to 52, rises to 58, then pulls back to 54: higher highs (55, 58) and higher lows (52, 54) mark an uptrend.

name: Downtrend
definition: A trend characterized by a series of descending peaks and troughs — successively lower highs and lower lows. It is the classical chart-based description of sustained supply exceeding demand; an analytical construct, not evidence that prices must keep falling.
intuition: Each rally stalls lower than the last and each drop breaks to a new floor — a staircase descending.
mechanics: Identified when each successive swing high forms below the prior swing high and each successive swing low breaks below the prior swing low. Often visualized with a down trendline connecting two or more falling highs; the downtrend is conventionally considered intact while price stays below that line or the last lower high.
failure_modes: Counter-trend rallies within downtrends can be sharp and prolonged, and are indistinguishable from genuine reversals until the structure confirms one way or the other.
misconceptions: That a downtrend means every bounce should be shorted immediately; bear-market rallies can retrace large portions of a decline before the downtrend resumes.
example: A stock falls from 100 to 90, bounces to 95, then falls to 88: lower highs (100, 95) and lower lows (90, 88) mark a downtrend.

name: Sideways market
definition: A market state in which prices oscillate within a horizontal band with roughly equal peaks and troughs, reflecting a balance between supply and demand rather than directional movement. Also described as consolidation or a ranging market; a descriptive label for price behavior, not a forecast.
intuition: Buyers and sellers are evenly matched, so price ping-pongs between an upper and a lower boundary.
mechanics: Identified when swing highs cluster near a common resistance level and swing lows near a common support level with no sustained progression in either direction. The state is considered resolved when price breaks decisively out of the band.
failure_modes: Range boundaries are approximate, so price frequently pokes through them intraday before returning, whipsawing traders who treat every touch of the edge as meaningful.
misconceptions: That sideways markets are low-risk because they are quiet; ranges often precede sharp directional moves, and volatility can expand abruptly.
example: A stock bounces between $70 support and $75 resistance for several weeks without closing outside the band.

name: Trading range
definition: A relatively tight horizontal price band, bounded by support below and resistance above, within which prices move while supply and demand are roughly balanced. In classical chart analysis a break of either boundary is taken as evidence that one side has gained control — a heuristic, not a law.
intuition: A tug-of-war zone: neither bulls nor bears can push price out of the box, until suddenly one side wins.
mechanics: Marked by drawing horizontal lines or zones at the range's reaction highs (resistance) and reaction lows (support); ranges can persist for weeks to months. Resolution is read from a decisive break of a boundary, ideally confirmed by expanding volume.
failure_modes: False breakouts at range boundaries are common; in wide or long-lived ranges the 'exact' levels are fuzzy enough that zone-based marking is more honest than single-price lines.
misconceptions: That merely touching a range boundary is a tradable signal; without confirmation, boundary touches and marginal breaks fail frequently.
example: ChartSchool documents WorldCom oscillating between support at 55 and resistance at 63 for about five months in 1999, including a false breakout above 62, before the range broke down through 55.

name: Swing high
definition: A local price peak — a high flanked by lower highs on either side — marking the point where an advance stalled and turned down. Swing highs (peaks) and swing lows (troughs) are the basic building blocks from which trend direction is read in classical technical analysis.
intuition: The top of one 'zig' before the market 'zags' back down.
mechanics: Discretionary analysts mark visible reaction peaks on the chart; rule-based definitions require a bar whose high exceeds the highs of a fixed number of bars on each side (e.g., two). Successive swing highs are compared — higher, lower, or equal — to classify trend structure, and old swing highs often serve as reference resistance.
failure_modes: The lookback that defines a swing is arbitrary, so different analysts mark different swings; minor swing highs are constantly exceeded and re-marked, making the concept scale-dependent.
misconceptions: That a swing high is a precise resistance price; it is better treated as an approximate zone, since technical analysis is not an exact science.
example: A stock rallies to 55, declines to 52, and rallies again: 55 is a swing high that later acts as a reference resistance level.

name: Swing low
definition: A local price trough — a low flanked by higher lows on either side — marking the point where a decline stalled and turned up. Swing lows (troughs), together with swing highs, form the price structure from which trend direction is read.
intuition: The bottom of one 'zag' before the market 'zigs' back up.
mechanics: Discretionary analysts mark visible reaction lows; rule-based definitions require a bar whose low is below the lows of a fixed number of bars on each side. Successive swing lows are compared to classify structure, and prior swing lows often serve as reference support or as stop-placement references.
failure_modes: As with swing highs, the defining lookback is arbitrary and the label is scale-dependent; marginal breaks of a swing low can be noise rather than structure change.
misconceptions: That a swing low must hold as support; prior lows are reference zones, not floors, and are routinely undercut before price reverses.
example: A stock drops to 48, rebounds to 52, then dips to 50: 48 is a swing low anchoring the emerging structure.

name: Higher high
definition: A swing high that exceeds the previous swing high. A sequence of higher highs combined with higher lows is the classical structural definition of an uptrend.
intuition: Each upward push reaches new territory, showing buyers keep gaining ground.
mechanics: Identified by comparing successive reaction peaks: when the latest peak trades or closes above the prior peak, a higher high is printed. Analysts track the sequence of highs and lows, rather than any single point, to judge whether trend structure remains intact.
failure_modes: A single higher high can be an exhaustion spike; without confirming higher lows the apparent bullish structure can invert immediately.
misconceptions: That printing one higher high confirms an uptrend; structure is a property of a sequence, and one peak in isolation means little.
example: After a pullback, a stock rallies past its old 55 peak to 58, printing a higher high that keeps the uptrend structure intact.

name: Higher low
definition: A swing low that forms above the previous swing low. Together with higher highs, a sequence of higher lows constitutes the structural definition of an uptrend and shows declining selling pressure on pullbacks.
intuition: Each dip finds buyers sooner than the last — the floor keeps rising.
mechanics: Identified by comparing successive reaction troughs: when the latest pullback low holds above the prior low, a higher low is printed. A break below the most recent higher low is conventionally treated as a warning that the uptrend structure may be changing.
failure_modes: Higher lows fail routinely as support on retest; a marginal undercut of the prior low can be stop-driven noise rather than a genuine structure break.
misconceptions: That a higher low is a safe, low-risk entry point by itself; it is a structural observation, not a signal with defined risk.
example: A stock pulls back to 54 after previously bottoming at 52, then rallies: the higher low at 54 preserves the uptrend structure.

name: Lower high
definition: A swing high that forms below the previous swing high. Together with lower lows, a sequence of lower highs constitutes the structural definition of a downtrend and shows weakening buying pressure on rallies.
intuition: Each bounce runs out of energy sooner than the last — the ceiling keeps sinking.
mechanics: Identified by comparing successive reaction peaks: when the latest rally high stalls below the prior peak, a lower high is printed. A break above the most recent lower high is conventionally treated as a warning that the downtrend structure may be changing.
failure_modes: Lower highs are frequently exceeded in bear-market rallies, which can retrace large portions of a decline before the downtrend resumes.
misconceptions: That a lower high guarantees further declines; it is one observation in a sequence and says nothing certain about the next move.
example: A stock in a downtrend bounces to 95 after previously peaking at 100, then rolls over: the lower high at 95 confirms sellers remain in control.

name: Lower low
definition: A swing low that breaks below the previous swing low. Together with lower highs, a sequence of lower lows constitutes the structural definition of a downtrend.
intuition: Each drop undercuts the last floor, showing sellers keep gaining ground.
mechanics: Identified by comparing successive reaction troughs: when the latest decline trades or closes below the prior trough, a lower low is printed. In an uptrend, a newly printed lower low is conventionally read as the first structural warning of a possible trend change.
failure_modes: Lower lows are often produced by stop-driven flushes that immediately recover; a marginal undercut does not by itself confirm a downtrend.
misconceptions: That a lower low in an uptrend proves the trend has reversed; it is a warning sign within a sequence, not a verdict.
example: A stock falls to 88 after previously bottoming at 90, printing a lower low that extends the downtrend's structure.

name: Support
definition: A price level or zone at which demand is thought to be strong enough to prevent the price from declining further. It is a core hypothesis of technical analysis about where buying interest concentrates, not a guaranteed floor.
intuition: As price gets cheaper, buyers become more willing to buy and sellers less willing to sell, so declines tend to pause there.
mechanics: Commonly established at previous reaction lows, broken resistance levels (polarity), round numbers, or moving averages. Because TA is not an exact science, practitioners often mark support as a zone rather than an exact price; a decisive break below is read as supply overcoming demand.
failure_modes: Support breaks happen regularly, especially in high volatility or around news; once broken, the old level can invert into resistance, trapping buyers who assumed it would hold.
misconceptions: That support is a precise price that must hold; brief dips below a level are common and do not necessarily invalidate it.
example: ChartSchool cites Halliburton returning repeatedly to support in the low 30s (October 1999 low near 31, December near 33, February near 32.5) before the level was tested again.

name: Resistance
definition: A price level or zone at which selling is thought to be strong enough to prevent the price from rising further. It is a core hypothesis of technical analysis about where supply concentrates, not a guaranteed ceiling.
intuition: As price gets more expensive, sellers become more willing to sell and buyers less willing to buy, so rallies tend to stall there.
mechanics: Commonly established at previous reaction highs or at broken support levels (polarity principle: broken support can turn into resistance and vice versa, often because trapped holders sell at breakeven on the return). A decisive break above is read as demand overcoming supply.
failure_modes: Resistance breaks happen regularly; price can also briefly exceed the level intraday and fall back, so marginal penetrations are unreliable as signals.
misconceptions: That resistance must repel price on the first approach; levels are zones of probable supply, and repeated tests often weaken them.
example: ChartSchool documents Halliburton's broken support at 42.5 turning into resistance: the stock rallied back to 42.5 three times and failed each time.

name: Breakout
definition: A price move above an established resistance level, range boundary, or chart-pattern upper boundary. In classical chart analysis a breakout is interpreted as evidence that demand has overcome supply at that level; it is an analytical reading, and a meaningful fraction of breakouts fail.
intuition: Price finally escapes the ceiling that had been capping it, suggesting buyers are now willing to pay more than before.
mechanics: Identified when price closes (or trades, depending on convention) above the watched level; confirmation heuristics include expanding volume, follow-through in subsequent sessions, and a successful retest of the broken level as new support.
failure_modes: False breakouts are frequent, especially on low volume; price pokes above the level, draws in breakout buyers, then closes back inside the old range.
misconceptions: That every break of resistance is the start of a new trend; without confirmation, single-bar breaks are routinely reversed.
example: ChartSchool documents WorldCom briefly poking above its 62 range resistance in mid-June 1999 — a breakout that failed within days and was nullified by a gap down.
source_hint: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending

name: Breakdown
definition: A price move below an established support level, range boundary, or chart-pattern lower boundary. In classical chart analysis a breakdown is interpreted as evidence that supply has overcome demand at that level; an analytical reading, not a certainty of further declines.
intuition: The floor that had been holding price up gives way, showing sellers are now willing to accept lower prices.
mechanics: Identified when price closes (or trades, by convention) below the watched support; a broken support level can subsequently act as resistance on rebounds (the polarity principle), and volume expansion is treated as confirmation.
failure_modes: Bear-trap breakdowns occur when price dips below support, triggers stops, and then reclaims the level; breakdowns on thin volume are especially unreliable.
misconceptions: That a support break must be followed by immediate collapse; markets frequently retest the broken level from below, offering a second exit before any sustained decline.
example: ChartSchool documents Lucent breaking support at 60 in late 1999 and falling so fast that exit above 44 was impossible — an illustration that breakdowns can gap through stops.

name: False breakout
definition: A breakout (or breakdown) that fails to hold: price moves beyond a watched level but cannot sustain itself there and closes back inside the prior range. It is the classical-TA label for a failed break; Smart Money Concepts frames the same event as a liquidity sweep.
intuition: Price teases a move out of the box, luring in breakout traders, then snaps back inside — trapping them on the wrong side.
mechanics: Identified only in retrospect: price trades beyond the level, then fails the follow-through test by closing back within the old range. Traders reduce exposure to false breaks by requiring closes beyond the level, volume confirmation, or a successful retest before acting.
failure_modes: The concept is inherently after-the-fact: at the moment of the break, a genuine breakout and a false breakout look identical, so filters that screen out false breaks also delay entry on real ones.
misconceptions: That false breakouts are always deliberate manipulation; the footprint is real, but intent cannot be proven from a chart.
example: ChartSchool's WorldCom example: price briefly poked above 62 resistance in mid-June 1999, then gapped back down days later, nullifying the breakout.

name: Retest
definition: The return of price to a level it has just broken, testing whether the old barrier now acts as the opposite kind — broken resistance as new support, or broken support as new resistance (the polarity principle). A successful retest is treated as confirmation of the break; a failed one warns of a false breakout.
intuition: After escaping the box, price comes back to check whether the old wall now works as a floor (or ceiling) from the other side.
mechanics: Observed when, following a break, price returns to the broken level and either respects it (holds beyond it, then resumes in the break direction) or fails (re-enters the old range). Many traders treat the retest, rather than the break itself, as the tradeable moment because it defines risk more tightly.
failure_modes: Retests do not always occur — strong moves may never look back; and a retest that holds can still fail later, since the polarity principle is a heuristic.
misconceptions: That a retest must touch the exact broken price; retests are zone affairs and may fall short or marginally overshoot the level.
example: ChartSchool documents the NASDAQ 100 breaking above 935 resistance in May 1997, then falling back to test 935 as support twice before advancing to 1150.

name: Pullback
definition: A temporary counter-move against the prevailing trend — typically shallow and short-lived — after which the prior trend resumes. It is an interpretive label: whether a counter-move is a pullback or the start of a reversal is knowable only in hindsight.
intuition: The trend takes a breather: some traders take profits, price slips a little, then the main move continues.
mechanics: Identified as a counter-trend decline in an uptrend (or rally in a downtrend) that stalls at logical areas such as prior support/resistance, moving averages, or Fibonacci retracement zones (often 38.2%-61.8%), and is followed by resumption of the trend. Volume commonly contracts during the pullback and expands on resumption.
failure_modes: Any pullback can deepen into a correction or full reversal; entering on the assumption of resumption fails precisely when the trend is ending.
misconceptions: That pullbacks are safe entries because 'the trend is intact'; trend integrity is only confirmed after the pullback resolves.
example: In an uptrend from 50 to 58, price dips back to 54 (near the 50% retracement and prior breakout level), forms a bullish candle, and then rallies to new highs.

name: Rally
definition: A period of sustained price increases over days to months. Rallies occur within both bull and bear markets; a rise within a dominant downtrend is a bear market rally — a counter-trend advance, not necessarily the start of a recovery.
intuition: A stretch where buyers dominate and prices climb, whether as the main trend or as a pause inside a larger decline.
mechanics: Identified simply as a sustained sequence of rising prices; context is what classifies it — a rally that keeps printing higher highs and higher lows within an uptrend is trend continuation, while a sharp multi-week rise under a falling primary trend is read as a potential bear market rally driven by short covering and oversold conditions.
failure_modes: Bear market rallies routinely suck in buyers and then fail at resistance, resuming the decline; only hindsight distinguishes them from new bull legs.
misconceptions: That a strong multi-week rally proves the bottom is in; 2022 produced several large bear market rallies that each resolved to new lows.
example: During the 2022 bear market, the S&P 500 staged several multi-week rallies amid Fed rate hikes; each faded and the downtrend resumed.

name: Correction
definition: A counter-trend decline within a prevailing uptrend, conventionally defined at the index level as a fall of 10% or more from the recent peak (but less than the 20% associated with a bear market). It is a descriptive, magnitude-based label applied to price action, not a forecast of what follows.
intuition: The market takes a meaningful step back inside a larger climb — deeper than a pullback, but short of a bear market.
mechanics: Measured as the percentage decline from the recent high: a drop of roughly 10% earns the label 'correction' by market convention; corrections are typically shorter in duration than bear markets and, in an intact bull trend, are followed by recovery to new highs.
formula: Correction depth (%) = (peak price - trough price) / peak price x 100; >= 10% is the conventional correction threshold, >= 20% the conventional bear market threshold.
failure_modes: The 10% threshold is arbitrary, and a correction can always deepen into a bear market; buying 'the correction' fails when the decline keeps going.
misconceptions: That a correction 'must' end near 10%; the label is retrospective, and nothing bounds the eventual depth at the time it is occurring.
example: The 2023-2024 bull market saw several ~10% declines (banking stress, AI concerns) that each recovered to new highs — textbook corrections within an uptrend.

name: Retracement
definition: A temporary reversal within a larger trend that gives back only part of the prior move before the trend resumes. The term is magnitude-focused — how much of the prior leg was retraced — and is usually measured in percentages (e.g., Fibonacci levels); it describes structure, not a prediction of resumption.
intuition: The market gives back a slice of what it just gained, then carries on — the question is always how big the slice will be.
mechanics: Measured as a percentage of the prior swing: retracement level = pivot high - (retracement % x (pivot high - pivot low)) for a pullback in an up-leg. Shallow retracements (~38.2%) are read as trend strength, deep ones (~61.8%-78.6%) as potential weakness or reversal risk.
formula: Retracement level = High - r x (High - Low) for an up-leg, where r is the retracement fraction (e.g., 0.382, 0.5, 0.618); symmetrically Low + r x (High - Low) for a down-leg.
failure_modes: There is no level a retracement must respect; a 'retracement' that exceeds 100% of the prior leg was in fact a reversal, which is only clear afterward.
misconceptions: That price is likely to stop at a particular retracement percentage; the percentages are observation conventions, and prices break through them regularly.
example: After a rally from 5809 to 6162 in S&P 500 futures, a decline to 5944 is a 61.8% retracement of the up-leg (6162.25 - 0.618 x 353.25 = 5944).

name: Reversal
definition: A durable change in the direction of the prevailing trend — an uptrend turning into a downtrend or vice versa — as opposed to a temporary counter-move. In chart analysis, reversals are confirmed through structure (broken swing sequences, broken trendlines, completed reversal patterns), and only after the fact with certainty.
intuition: The tide actually turns: what was a staircase up becomes a staircase down.
mechanics: Read from structure shifts: in an uptrend, a lower high followed by a lower low (breaking the last higher low) signals a possible reversal; trendline breaks, support/resistance breaks, and classical reversal patterns (double tops/bottoms, head and shoulders) provide corroboration. Depth and duration distinguish reversal from pullback or consolidation.
failure_modes: Early reversal signals frequently turn out to be deep pullbacks; acting on the first structural break exposes the trader to trend resumption.
misconceptions: That reversals can be called at the turn; every real-time 'reversal call' is a probabilistic bet, and counter-trend calling is a classic account destroyer.
example: An uptrend printing 55, 58 highs and 52, 54 lows breaks down through 54, then rallies only to 56 (lower high) and falls under 52: the reversed sequence confirms a trend change.

name: Continuation
definition: The resumption of the prevailing trend after a pause, pullback, or consolidation. In classical chart analysis, continuation is the default expectation associated with congestion patterns and mid-trend gaps — a probabilistic heuristic, not a law.
intuition: The trend catches its breath and then keeps going in the same direction.
mechanics: Identified when a counter-move or sideways congestion resolves with a break in the direction of the prior trend — e.g., a consolidation range breaking with the trend, or a runaway (continuation) gap appearing mid-trend on rising volume.
failure_modes: Not every pause continues the trend — some consolidations are distribution or accumulation that precede reversals, so continuation assumptions fail at trend turning points.
misconceptions: That a pause in a trend guarantees continuation; continuation is the base-rate expectation, but each individual congestion can resolve either way.
example: A stock trending up pauses in a two-week sideways range, then gaps higher on increased volume — a continuation resolution of the congestion.

name: Consolidation
definition: A period during which price moves sideways within a relatively contained range after a prior move, reflecting a temporary balance between buyers and sellers. Consolidations are read as pauses that can resolve into either continuation or reversal; the label describes the pause, not its outcome.
intuition: After running, the market rests — price churns in a band while both sides regroup.
mechanics: Identified as a stretch of overlapping bars bounded by approximate horizontal support and resistance, often with contracting volume and range. Resolution is read from the direction of the eventual range break, ideally confirmed by volume expansion.
failure_modes: Consolidations produce repeated false breaks at their edges before resolving; the longer the range, the fuzzier its exact boundaries.
misconceptions: That consolidation means the trend will continue ('a pause that refreshes'); it can equally mark distribution before a reversal.
example: After rallying from 27 to 64, WorldCom consolidated between 55 and 63 for about five months in 1999 before breaking down through 55 (ChartSchool case study).

name: Compression
definition: A progressive narrowing of price swings and trading ranges, reflecting falling volatility as buyers and sellers reach a temporary equilibrium. In volatility-based frameworks (e.g., Bollinger Bands), compression is associated with the 'squeeze' state that often — but not reliably — precedes a directional expansion.
intuition: Price action coils like a spring: swings get smaller and smaller until the stored energy releases in a sharp move.
mechanics: Observed as successively smaller bar ranges and converging swing highs/lows; quantified with volatility measures such as narrowing Bollinger Bands (which contract as the standard deviation of price falls) or falling ATR/BandWidth readings.
failure_modes: Compression says nothing about direction, and squeezes can persist far longer than expected or resolve in a fakeout before the true move.
misconceptions: That compression must resolve in a large move; low-volatility regimes can persist indefinitely, and the eventual break can be small.
example: A stock's daily ranges shrink over three weeks while its Bollinger Bands narrow to their tightest width in months, preceding a sharp breakout.

name: Expansion
definition: A broadening of price swings and bar ranges, reflecting rising volatility as one side of the market gains decisive control. It is the counterpart of compression and typically accompanies breakouts, breakdowns, and trend acceleration.
intuition: The coiled spring releases: small quiet bars give way to large directional ones.
mechanics: Observed as enlarging bar ranges and directional closes, often from a prior consolidation; quantified by widening Bollinger Bands (bands expand as the standard deviation of price rises) or rising ATR/BandWidth.
failure_modes: Expansion driven by news spikes can be one-bar events that immediately mean-revert; chasing expansion late buys the extreme of the move.
misconceptions: That expansion confirms a durable new trend; an initial volatility burst can be exhaustion rather than initiation.
example: After weeks of narrow ranges, a stock prints consecutive wide-range up bars on heavy volume as it breaks out of its base — a volatility expansion phase.

name: Volatility contraction
definition: A measurable decline in price volatility — shrinking bar ranges, falling standard deviation, narrowing volatility bands — typically during consolidation. Frameworks such as Bollinger's squeeze treat contraction as a precondition that often precedes a volatility expansion, a statistical tendency rather than a law.
intuition: The market goes quiet: each day's high-low span shrinks as price compresses into a tighter and tighter zone.
mechanics: Quantified with indicators such as Bollinger BandWidth (which falls as the bands contract with declining standard deviation), ATR, or historical volatility; identified visually as progressively smaller bars and converging swings.
failure_modes: Contraction gives no directional information and no timing guarantee; volatility can stay depressed long after a squeeze registers.
misconceptions: That a volatility contraction must be followed by an explosive move; the tendency is documented, but individual squeezes frequently fizzle.
example: A stock's 20-day Bollinger Bands narrow to multi-month lows during a flat consolidation — the classic 'squeeze' setup watched for a subsequent break.
source_hint: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending
review_note: The 'volatility contraction pattern' as a named trading setup (Minervini's VCP) has no canonical published formula; the measurable core (falling standard deviation / band width) is what is cited here.

name: Volatility expansion
definition: A measurable increase in price volatility — widening bar ranges, rising standard deviation, expanding volatility bands — typically accompanying breakouts and trend legs. It is the mirror of volatility contraction and marks regimes where price travels further per unit time.
intuition: The quiet market wakes up: bars get longer and price starts covering ground fast.
mechanics: Quantified by rising Bollinger BandWidth (bands widen automatically as the standard deviation of price increases), rising ATR, or rising historical volatility; observed visually as a sequence of wide-range directional bars.
failure_modes: Volatility expansion cuts both ways: it raises opportunity and risk simultaneously, and late entries during expansion phases suffer the widest adverse excursions.
misconceptions: That expanding volatility is bullish; it is direction-neutral — crashes are volatility expansions too.
example: A stock breaking out of a months-long base prints daily ranges three times its recent average, and its Bollinger Bands widen sharply as the new trend leg begins.

name: Gap
definition: A blank space on a price chart where no trading occurred between two consecutive bars — typically when the open of one session is entirely above the prior session's high (up gap) or below its low (down gap). Gaps are classified (common, breakaway, runaway, exhaustion) by location and context; the classifications are interpretive, not mechanical laws.
intuition: Overnight news or sentiment shifts the supply-demand balance so much that the market has to reopen at a different price entirely, skipping the levels in between.
mechanics: Detected by comparing one bar's range to the next: an up gap requires the new session's low to exceed the prior session's high; a down gap requires the new session's high to fall below the prior session's low. Significance is judged by size, volume, and position within the trend or pattern.
failure_modes: Gap-type labels are only reliably assignable in hindsight (an exhaustion gap looks like a runaway gap when it prints); the popular belief that 'all gaps get filled' fails badly for breakaway and runaway gaps.
misconceptions: That every gap must soon be filled; waiting for breakaway or runaway gaps to fill can mean missing or fighting an entire trend leg.
example: A stock closes at 50, reports strong earnings after the bell, and opens the next day at 54, never trading below 53.8: the 50-53.8 void is an up gap.

name: Gap up
definition: A gap in which a session's low is higher than the previous session's high, leaving an untraded void below the new session's range. Generally read as a sign of strong buying interest; its analytical meaning depends on where in the trend or pattern it occurs.
intuition: Demand overwhelmed supply overnight, so the market had to reopen above yesterday's entire trading range.
mechanics: Identified when today's low exceeds yesterday's high on the chart. Interpretation follows gap typology: in a congestion area it may be a common gap, breaking out of a range a breakaway gap, mid-trend a runaway gap, and late in an extended move a possible exhaustion gap.
failure_modes: Gap ups into extended moves can be exhaustion gaps that mark the top; and opening gaps that fail to hold through the close are just intraday volatility, not structural gaps.
misconceptions: That a gap up is automatically bullish follow-through fuel; context decides, and faded gaps are a daily occurrence in thin markets.
example: After weeks of consolidation, a stock gaps above its range resistance on heavy volume following earnings — a bullish breakaway-style gap up.

name: Gap down
definition: A gap in which a session's high is lower than the previous session's low, leaving an untraded void above the new session's range. Generally read as a sign of strong selling pressure; its analytical meaning depends on where in the trend or pattern it occurs.
intuition: Supply overwhelmed demand overnight, so the market had to reopen below yesterday's entire trading range.
mechanics: Identified when today's high falls below yesterday's low. Interpretation follows gap typology: common gap inside congestion, breakaway gap on a range breakdown, runaway gap mid-downtrend, or exhaustion gap late in an extended decline.
failure_modes: Gap downs late in a decline can be exhaustion gaps that mark capitulation lows; intraday-only gaps that do not hold into the close carry no structural significance.
misconceptions: That a gap down guarantees further downside; panic gap downs are frequently filled quickly as the selling exhausts itself.
example: A stock in a trading range gaps below range support on heavy volume after a profit warning — a bearish breakaway-style gap down.

name: Exhaustion gap
definition: A gap occurring near the end of an extended up or down move, typically on very high volume and a large price jump, interpreted as the final surge of euphoria or panic before the move ends. The label is only assignable with confidence in hindsight, since at the time it can be indistinguishable from a runaway gap.
intuition: The last burst of FOMO buying (or panic selling) — the crowd all rushes in at once, and then there is nobody left to push further.
mechanics: Identified by context: a gap late in a prolonged trend, accompanied by exceptionally high volume and often a wide open-to-close range, followed quickly by the gap being filled as price reverses. ChartSchool notes the exceptionally high volume is what separates it from a runaway gap.
failure_modes: Mistaking a runaway gap for an exhaustion gap leads to premature counter-trend positioning; the two look identical at print time and are separated mainly by what volume and follow-through do next.
misconceptions: That any big late-trend gap is exhaustion; trends can produce several large gaps before truly exhausting.
example: After a long advance, a stock gaps up on huge volume, stalls as profit-taking dries up demand, and within days fills the gap and reverses — the exhaustion signature.

name: Breakaway gap
definition: A gap that occurs as price breaks out of a trading range or congestion area, interpreted as marking the start of a new directional move. Breakaway gaps are conventionally expected NOT to be filled soon, distinguishing them from common gaps; the classification remains an interpretive heuristic.
intuition: The market escapes its cage in one jump — enthusiasm is so strong that price skips the boundary levels entirely.
mechanics: Identified by location (at the boundary of a congestion area or chart pattern) and by volume, which should pick up significantly. The breakout point is then expected to act as new support (upside break) or resistance (downside break); a prompt fill argues against the breakaway reading.
failure_modes: A gap out of a range that is quickly filled was a false breakout with extra steps; low-volume breakaway gaps are especially suspect.
misconceptions: That a breakaway gap will soon be filled, offering a better entry; the whole point of the classification is that waiting for the fill often means missing the move.
example: ChartSchool's example: after weeks of consolidation and a low-volume poke above resistance, a stock gaps up on high volume, starting a new uptrend — a breakaway gap.

name: Runaway gap
definition: A gap occurring in the middle of an established trend, driven by a sudden surge of interest (or liquidation) in the trend's direction, and interpreted as evidence the trend is accelerating rather than ending. Also called a measuring gap, from the heuristic that it tends to appear roughly halfway through a move.
intuition: Traders who waited for a pullback give up waiting and pile in all at once, gapping price further along the trend.
mechanics: Identified by location mid-trend with a notable volume increase during and after the gap. The measuring heuristic projects the remaining move as approximately equal to the move from the trend's start to the gap.
formula: Measuring heuristic: projected objective approximately equals gap price plus (gap price minus move origin) for an up-move; a rule of thumb, not a validated formula.
failure_modes: The halfway-point measuring heuristic fails routinely, and a supposed runaway gap can turn out to be the exhaustion gap that ends the move.
misconceptions: That mid-trend gaps are safe to chase; runaway gaps in downtrends reflect liquidation cascades where price must fall further to find buyers, and entries against them are dangerous.
example: A stock in a strong uptrend gaps up mid-move on surging volume as sidelined traders stop waiting for a retracement — the classic runaway gap described by ChartSchool.

name: Common gap
definition: A small, uneventful gap occurring within a trading range or congestion area, typically on low volume (e.g., around ex-dividend dates), with no trend significance. Common gaps are usually filled quickly.
intuition: A mundane hiccup in an already quiet market — price skips a few ticks and nobody much cares.
mechanics: Identified by context rather than size: the gap appears inside an existing range or congestion area on unremarkable volume. Because the range itself is expected to contain price, the gap is normally retraced ('filled') within days to weeks.
failure_modes: The main risk is misclassification — treating a genuine breakaway gap as a common gap and fading a real breakout.
misconceptions: That all gaps are meaningful signals; common gaps in thin securities are closer to noise and offer little trading information.
example: A thinly traded stock goes ex-dividend and opens slightly lower inside its range, leaving a small gap that is filled within the week — a common gap.

name: Trendline
definition: A straight line drawn on a chart connecting two or more price points and extended forward, used to visualize a trend and to act as a dynamic reference for support (up trendline, connecting rising lows) or resistance (down trendline, connecting falling highs). It is a discretionary drawing tool, not an objective market feature.
intuition: Connect the dots of the trend's pullbacks, and the resulting line sketches the trend's natural floor (or ceiling).
mechanics: An up trendline connects two or more ascending lows (the second low must exceed the first); a down trendline connects two or more descending highs. More touches without a break are taken as evidence of significance; a close beyond the line is a warning that the trend may be changing, to be confirmed by other evidence.
failure_modes: Placement is subjective — different analysts draw different lines on the same chart; trendline breaks generate frequent false warnings, especially on steep or shallow trends.
misconceptions: That a trendline break proves the trend has reversed; Fidelity itself cautions it should serve only as a warning requiring confirmation.
example: Connecting the pullback lows at 50, 52, and 54 in a rising stock yields an up trendline; price bouncing off the line a fourth time is read as the uptrend remaining intact.

name: Channel
definition: A chart structure formed by two parallel trendlines that enclose price action: a primary trendline along the trend's pullbacks and a parallel channel (return) line along the opposite swings. Channels frame trend direction plus likely reaction zones; they are descriptive constructs, not predictive guarantees.
intuition: Price travels between two parallel rails — one rail supports it, the other caps it — until it jumps the track.
mechanics: Draw the trendline through the trend's lows (uptrend) or highs (downtrend), then draw a parallel line through the opposite extreme(s). Traders reference the lower line as support and the upper as resistance; breaks of either rail are read as acceleration or potential trend change depending on direction.
failure_modes: True parallel structure is rarer than textbooks suggest; forced parallelism produces channels that price ignores, and channel breaks fail like any other level break.
misconceptions: That price must reverse at the channel rails; strong trends ride one rail for extended periods, and breaks of the far rail often accelerate rather than reverse the move.
example: A rising stock respects a rising support line at its pullback lows while a parallel line through its rally highs caps each advance, forming an ascending channel.

name: Ascending channel
definition: A channel whose two parallel boundary lines slope upward, enclosing an uptrend's higher highs and higher lows. The lower (support) line connects rising lows and the parallel upper (resistance) line caps the rallies; classically read as trend-consistent structure until broken.
intuition: An uptrend with guardrails: each dip bounces off the lower rail, each push fades near the upper rail.
mechanics: Constructed by drawing an up trendline through two or more rising swing lows and a parallel line through the intervening swing high(s). Range-trading heuristics buy near the lower rail and take profits near the upper; a break below the lower rail warns of trend change.
failure_modes: Upside breaks of the upper rail can be climactic exhaustion moves; downside breaks of the support rail during what looked like orderly ascent catch range traders long at the top rail.
misconceptions: That an ascending channel is purely bullish; a downside break of its support rail is a recognized reversal warning, and rising channels in weak trends often fail downward.
example: A stock's pullbacks bottom on a rising line through 50, 53, 56 while rallies stall on the parallel line through 55, 58, 61 — an ascending channel.

name: Descending channel
definition: A channel whose two parallel boundary lines slope downward, enclosing a downtrend's lower highs and lower lows. The upper (resistance) line connects falling highs and the parallel lower (support) line floors the declines; classically read as trend-consistent structure until broken.
intuition: A downtrend with guardrails: each bounce dies at the upper rail, each drop finds footing near the lower rail.
mechanics: Constructed by drawing a down trendline through two or more falling swing highs and a parallel line through the intervening swing low(s). Heuristics sell rallies near the upper rail and cover near the lower; a break above the upper rail warns of trend change.
failure_modes: Downside breaks of the lower rail can be capitulation spikes that immediately reverse; upside breaks catch shorts who assumed the rails would hold.
misconceptions: That a descending channel is purely bearish; an upside break of its resistance rail is a recognized reversal warning.
example: A stock's bounces stall on a falling line through 100, 95, 90 while declines bottom on the parallel line through 92, 87, 82 — a descending channel.

name: Horizontal channel
definition: A channel whose two parallel boundary lines are roughly horizontal, enclosing a sideways market: resistance above and support below at approximately constant prices. It represents consolidation or indecision and is the channel equivalent of a trading range.
intuition: Price bounces between a flat floor and a flat ceiling while the market makes up its mind.
mechanics: Constructed by drawing a horizontal line across the reaction highs and a parallel horizontal line across the reaction lows. Range-trading heuristics buy support and sell resistance until a decisive breakout occurs; the direction of the eventual break is treated as the resolution signal.
failure_modes: Horizontal channels produce repeated false breaks at both rails; tight stops just outside the rails are exactly where whipsaws cluster.
misconceptions: That a horizontal channel's eventual break is equally likely up or down in all contexts; prior trend and volume behavior skew the odds, though never to certainty.
example: A stock oscillates between 70 support and 75 resistance for weeks, forming a horizontal channel, until a high-volume close above 75 resolves it upward.

name: Fibonacci retracement
definition: A charting technique that marks horizontal levels at percentages of a prior price swing — conventionally 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%, and 78.6% (ratios derived from the Fibonacci sequence, except 50%, a Dow Theory convention) — as candidate support/resistance zones for a counter-trend move. It is an analytical framework with no established predictive validity on its own.
intuition: If trends tend to give back part of a move before resuming, these ratios are the conventional yardsticks for how much.
mechanics: The analyst selects a swing low and swing high; the platform draws levels at the fixed percentages of that range. In an uptrend the levels below the high are watched as pullback support; in a downtrend, as rally resistance. Shallow (38.2%) retracements are read as trend strength, deep (61.8%-78.6%) as reversal risk.
formula: Retracement level (up-leg) = High - r x (High - Low), with r in {0.236, 0.382, 0.5, 0.618, 0.786}; e.g., High 6162.25, Low 5809 gives the 61.8% level at 6162.25 - 0.618 x 353.25 = 5944.00.
failure_modes: Swing-point selection is subjective, so different analysts get different levels; prices break through Fibonacci levels routinely, and the tool is unreliable in choppy, trendless markets.
misconceptions: That the ratios have a natural or mathematical claim on market behavior; any efficacy is usually attributed to self-fulfilling order clustering, and critics note confirmation bias in how levels are applied.
example: S&P 500 e-mini futures, January 2025 (Investopedia worked example): pivot high 6162.25, pivot low 5809; the 61.8% retracement level is computed at 5944.00 and watched as potential pullback support.

name: Fibonacci extension
definition: A charting technique that projects levels beyond the prior swing — conventionally 100%, 161.8%, and 261.8% of the measured move — as candidate profit-target or exhaustion zones once the trend resumes. Like retracements, it is an analytical convention, not a validated forecasting law.
intuition: If the retracement yardstick measures how far price pulls back, the extension yardstick guesses how far the next leg might reach.
mechanics: Applied after a trend resumes: the prior swing's range (or the swing plus its retracement, in three-point projection tools) is multiplied by extension ratios and projected past the old extreme. The 161.8% projection is the most widely watched target.
formula: Extension level (up-move) = Low + e x (High - Low) with e > 1 (e.g., 1.618); three-point variant: target = RetracementLow + e x (High - Low).
failure_modes: All the subjectivity of retracements applies, compounded by the choice of anchor points; trends frequently stop well short of, or blow through, projected extensions.
misconceptions: That extension targets are high-probability exit prices; they are reference zones at best, and many moves never reach the 161.8% projection.
example: After a stock rallies 40 to 50 and resumes upward from a 46 pullback, the 161.8% extension of the 40-50 leg projects a target zone near 62.2 (46 + 1.618 x 10).

name: Pivot point
definition: A calculated price level derived from the prior period's high, low, and close, used to frame the current period's directional bias and to derive support/resistance levels. Originating with floor traders, pivot points are deterministic calculations; their use as turning-point levels is a convention, not a validated edge.
intuition: Yesterday's average price becomes today's line in the sand: above it leans bullish, below it leans bearish.
mechanics: The base pivot P = (High + Low + Close)/3 of the prior period; derived levels include S1 = 2P - High, S2 = P - (High - Low), R1 = 2P - Low, R2 = P + (High - Low). Levels are computed once per period and remain fixed; variants include Fibonacci and Demark pivots.
formula: P = (H + L + C)/3; S1 = 2P - H; S2 = P - (H - L); R1 = 2P - L; R2 = P + (H - L), where H, L, C are the prior period's high, low, close.
failure_modes: In strongly trending periods price may never interact with the pivot, and in whippy markets it slices through the levels repeatedly; the levels have no inherent causal force.
misconceptions: That pivot levels are precise reversal points; ChartSchool treats them as a framework to be confirmed with price action and other indicators.
example: Yesterday's H/L/C are 105, 99, 102: P = 102, R1 = 105, S1 = 99. A move above 102 early today is read as positive, targeting R1 at 105.

name: Daily pivot
definition: A pivot point computed from the previous trading day's high, low, and close, applied to the current day's trading — the original floor-trader usage. On StockCharts' convention, pivots for 1- to 15-minute intraday charts use the prior day's data and remain fixed all day.
intuition: Yesterday's H/L/C distill into today's map of where buyers and sellers are expected to contest control.
mechanics: Computed at the start of the day as P = (prior day H + L + C)/3 with the standard derived S1/S2/R1/R2 levels; the levels do not change intraday and are used as bias filter (price above or below P) and as support/resistance references.
formula: P = (H_prev_day + L_prev_day + C_prev_day)/3; S1 = 2P - H; R1 = 2P - L; S2 = P - (H - L); R2 = P + (H - L).
failure_modes: Gap openings can start the day far beyond the pivot, making the levels irrelevant; quiet range days slice back and forth across P, generating noise.
misconceptions: That daily pivots are intraday reversal guarantees; they are reference levels whose reactions must be confirmed.
example: An index future closes at 5000 with a 5030 high and 4970 low; today's daily pivot set is P = 5000, R1 = 5030, S1 = 4970, watched on the 5-minute chart all session.
source_hint: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending

name: Weekly pivot
definition: A pivot point computed from the previous calendar week's high, low, and close, applied to the current week. On StockCharts' convention, pivots for 30- to 120-minute charts use the prior week's data and remain fixed for the entire week.
intuition: Last week's price action condenses into this week's bias line and outer reference levels.
mechanics: Computed at the week's start as P = (prior week H + L + C)/3 with derived S/R levels; fixed for the week and recalculated on the first trading day of the next week.
formula: P = (H_prev_week + L_prev_week + C_prev_week)/3; S1 = 2P - H; R1 = 2P - L; S2 = P - (H - L); R2 = P + (H - L).
failure_modes: Same structural limits as all pivots: strong weekly trends can leave the pivot behind on day one, and holiday-shortened weeks distort the inputs.
misconceptions: That weekly pivots are more 'reliable' than daily ones by nature; they are merely slower-moving references with the same heuristic status.
example: Last week a stock printed H 110, L 100, C 108: this week's weekly pivot is P = 106, with R1 = 112 and S1 = 102 on the 60-minute chart.
source_hint: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending

name: Monthly pivot
definition: A pivot point computed from the previous month's high, low, and close, applied to the current month. On StockCharts' convention, pivots displayed on daily charts use the prior month's data and remain fixed for the whole month (weekly and monthly charts use the prior year's data).
intuition: Last month's range and close set this month's reference grid for where longer-term buyers and sellers may engage.
mechanics: Computed on the first trading day of the month as P = (prior month H + L + C)/3 with derived S/R levels; fixed until the next month begins, and used on daily charts as slower bias and support/resistance references.
formula: P = (H_prev_month + L_prev_month + C_prev_month)/3; S1 = 2P - H; R1 = 2P - L; S2 = P - (H - L); R2 = P + (H - L).
failure_modes: Monthly levels are coarse on volatile instruments, often sitting far from price and untouched for weeks; gaps between months can strand the grid entirely.
misconceptions: That monthly pivots carry institutional weight by construction; they are arithmetic averages of last month's range, watched only by those who choose to watch them.
example: A stock printed H 120, L 100, C 115 in May: June's monthly pivot is P = 111.67, plotted on the daily chart for all of June.

name: Market structure break
definition: In price-structure analysis, a break of the swing sequence defining the current trend: in an uptrend, a close below the most recent higher low (or, in continuation terms, a close above the prior swing high that extends the structure). SMC/ICT usage distinguishes a trend-continuing break of structure from a counter-trend structure shift; the terminology is a discretionary convention without a single canonical authority.
intuition: The market's staircase pattern breaks a step — the rhythm of higher floors or lower ceilings is violated, so the structure may be changing.
mechanics: Map swing highs and lows; a trend-continuing BOS prints when price exceeds the last swing high in an uptrend (or undercuts the last swing low in a downtrend), while a structure break against the trend prints when the last higher low (or lower high) is taken out. Confirmation conventions vary: some require a close beyond the swing, others a wick.
failure_modes: Marginal wick-throughs of a swing look like structure breaks but resolve as stop runs; and without a fixed swing-definition rule, two analysts mark different structures on the same chart.
misconceptions: That a single broken swing proves trend reversal; a wick through a level that closes back inside is a sweep, not a break — acceptance beyond the level is the distinguishing test.
example: An uptrend with higher lows at 50, 52, 54 breaks down when price closes below 54: the structure break flips bias from buying dips to selling rallies.

name: Change of character
definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the first structural break against the prevailing trend — e.g., in an uptrend, the first close below a higher low — read as an early signal that order flow may be shifting. It is the counter-trend counterpart of a trend-continuing break of structure; a discretionary convention with no canonical authority.
intuition: The first crack in the trend's rhythm: the market does something it hasn't been doing, hinting the character of the move is changing.
mechanics: After establishing the trend's swing sequence, mark the most recent higher low (uptrend) or lower high (downtrend); a decisive break of that pivot against the trend is the change of character. SMC models typically require a preceding liquidity sweep and subsequent displacement before treating it as tradable evidence.
failure_modes: CHoCH signals proliferate on lower timeframes and most are noise within higher-timeframe trends; deep pullbacks routinely trigger counter-trend structure breaks without reversing the main trend.
misconceptions: That a CHoCH is a sell/buy signal by itself; within SMC it is context requiring confirmation (displacement, a return to an order block or gap), not an entry trigger.
example: After a sweep of the prior high, an uptrending pair closes below its last higher low on the 15-minute chart — a CHoCH that SMC traders take as the first evidence of a possible short-side shift.

Definition reflects the best available exposition (LuxAlgo Library); conventions vary between practitioners.

name: Liquidity sweep
definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, a run through a level where resting orders cluster — stop-losses and breakout entries just beyond an obvious high or low — followed by failure to hold beyond it: price trades through, fills those orders, and closes back inside the prior range. The same chart event is called a false breakout in classical TA; 'sweep' adds an interpretation (order collection) that a chart cannot prove.
intuition: Price pokes through an obvious level, triggers the crowd's stops, then snaps back — the level was the target of the move, not an obstacle in its way.
mechanics: Identification is a two-part check: mark pools where stops cluster (prior swing highs/lows, equal highs/lows, session extremes), then require the failure — a trade through the level (often on a wick) followed by a close back inside the old range. A close that holds beyond the level with continuation is a breakout, not a sweep.
failure_modes: At the moment of the break a sweep and a genuine breakout are indistinguishable — only the close and follow-through separate them, so acting early means sometimes fading real breakouts.
misconceptions: That sweeps prove a market maker deliberately hunted retail stops; order-flow research documents stop clustering at predictable levels, but intent is narrative, not observable fact.
example: Price wicks above a prior swing high where buy stops rest, immediately rejects, and closes back inside the range; SMC traders read the level as swept and look for short setups on the retrace.
source_hint: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending
review_note: No primary/canonical source exists for SMC/ICT terminology; definition reflects the best available exposition (LuxAlgo Library). Edge definitions are contested (wick-through vs required close back inside).

name: Stop run
definition: A move that pushes price through a level where stop-loss orders are known or presumed to cluster, triggering them, often followed by a quick reversal. In SMC vocabulary this is the liquidity sweep; in classical terms it overlaps with the false breakout. The deliberate-targeting framing is an inference, not an observable fact.
intuition: Obvious levels have crowds of stops parked behind them; a push through sets off that cascade in one quick burst.
mechanics: Identified by the footprint: a fast trade through a well-watched swing high/low or round number, a burst of activity as stops execute, and (in the sweep reading) failure to hold beyond the level. Buy stops sit above highs, sell stops below lows, so the run direction names the pool being executed.
failure_modes: Not every run through a level reverses — sometimes the stop cascade fuels a genuine breakout; distinguishing the two requires waiting for the close and follow-through.
misconceptions: That brokers or market makers visibly hunt individual retail stops; academic work documents stop clustering and unusual behavior at such levels, but the personalized stop-hunt story is contested.
example: A pair trades two ticks below an obvious equal-lows level, triggering clustered sell stops, then closes back above the level within the same bar — a classic stop-run footprint.

name: Supply zone
definition: A price band marking the base from which a strong decline launched, drawn (in supply-and-demand methodology) around the small consolidation preceding the impulsive drop. It is treated as potential resistance on a return, on the hypothesis that unfilled sell interest remains there — a discretionary zone framework related to, but looser than, classical resistance.
intuition: Price paused, then fell out of bed; the pause zone is where sellers were last in control, so the first return there may meet them again.
mechanics: Identify an impulsive decline; step back to the small base candles just before it. Draw the zone around the base — proximal line at the edge nearest current price, distal line at the base's extreme — and extend it right. Reversal zones (rally-base-drop) form at swing turns; continuation zones (drop-base-drop) form mid-swing.
failure_modes: Zones are re-drawn to fit hindsight, and price trades straight through many of them; continuation-type (RBR/DBD) zones are documented by practitioners as weaker than reversal-type zones.
misconceptions: That a supply zone is proof of institutional sell orders waiting there; the zone marks where price left a base impulsively, and the unfilled-orders story is an inference, not an observation.
example: EUR/USD pauses for three small candles at 1.0850-1.0860, then drops 100 pips; the base is drawn as a supply zone and watched for a short entry on the first return.

name: Demand zone
definition: A price band marking the base from which a strong advance launched, drawn (in supply-and-demand methodology) around the small consolidation preceding the impulsive rally. It is treated as potential support on a return, on the hypothesis that unfilled buy interest remains there — a discretionary zone framework related to, but looser than, classical support.
intuition: Price paused, then took off upward; the pause zone is where buyers were last in control, so the first return there may attract them again.
mechanics: Identify an impulsive rally; step back to the small base candles just before it and box the base (proximal edge nearest current price, distal edge at the base extreme). Reversal zones (drop-base-rally) form at swing lows; continuation zones (rally-base-rally) form mid-swing and are regarded by practitioners as weaker.
failure_modes: Zone boundaries are subjective and hindsight-fitted; price frequently slices through demand zones without reacting, especially continuation-type zones formed mid-swing.
misconceptions: That an untouched ('fresh') demand zone must hold on first test; freshness heuristics are practitioner rules of thumb without validated statistics.
example: GBP/JPY bases at 182.00-182.30, then rallies sharply; the base is drawn as a demand zone, and a later retracement into it produces a bullish engulfing entry.

name: Order block
definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the last opposite-direction candle (or consecutive cluster of them) before an impulsive move — the final down candle before a rally (bullish) or the final up candle before a decline (bearish) — marked as a zone that may be defended on a return. It is read as the footprint of institutional position-building; that reading is an interpretation, since the candle alone shows only price, not orders.
intuition: The last place price sat before the big move launched is treated as the move's origin — and origins are where defenders may remain.
mechanics: Find the displacement first (an impulsive leg that breaks structure or sweeps a swing, ideally leaving a fair value gap), then step back to the last opposite close and box its range — conventions include full high-low, body only, or the 50% mean threshold. A decisive close through the whole zone invalidates it; the failed zone is then watched as a 'breaker' from the other side.
failure_modes: Candidate blocks are everywhere, so most are meaningless; price trades straight through a large share of them, and there is no reliable published hit rate for the concept.
misconceptions: That an order block visibly shows institutional orders; only the candle is observable, and the institutional-footprint narrative cannot be verified from the chart.
example: A pair sweeps a low, then rallies impulsively through the prior swing high; the last down-close candle before that leg is boxed as a bullish order block, watched for longs on the retrace (mitigation).

name: Fair value gap
definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, a three-candle pattern in which the middle candle's range does not overlap with the wicks of its neighbors — the low of the third candle sits above the high of the first (bullish FVG), or the high of the third sits below the low of the first (bearish FVG) — leaving a span price crossed in a single fast pass. It is read as an inefficiency that price may later revisit; that expectation is a hypothesis, not an established regularity.
intuition: The middle candle moved so fast that a slice of prices was skipped; the gap marks the skipped slice.
mechanics: Scan consecutive three-candle sequences: for a bullish FVG, check whether candle 3's low exceeds candle 1's high — the gap is the void between them. Traders mark the span (sometimes refined to its midpoint, the 'consequent encroachment') and watch for a retracement into it as entry context, with invalidation beyond the gap's far edge.
formula: Bullish FVG exists when Low(candle3) > High(candle1); gap span = [High(candle1), Low(candle3)]. Bearish FVG exists when High(candle3) < Low(candle1); span = [High(candle3), Low(candle1)].
failure_modes: FVGs are extremely common, especially on low timeframes, so most carry no information; many are never filled, and 'price returns to balance inefficiencies' is an untested slogan rather than a documented tendency.
misconceptions: That an FVG must be filled; unlike session gaps (where 'gap fill' at least has a mechanical definition), there is no validated fill-rate for FVGs, and the concept repackages older notions of price vacuums.
example: Candle 1 tops at 100.20, candle 2 surges to close at 102, and candle 3 bottoms at 101.50: the 100.20-101.50 span is a bullish fair value gap watched for support on a retrace.

name: Imbalance zone
definition: A chart region where price moved so quickly in one direction that little two-sided trading occurred — operationalized in SMC/ICT practice chiefly as the fair value gap, the three-candle non-overlap span. The zone is hypothesized to attract a later revisit ('rebalancing'); the hypothesis is discretionary and unproven.
intuition: A one-sided stampede leaves thin ice on the chart — a stretch where almost no business was done.
mechanics: Identified as the span between the first and third candles' non-overlapping wicks in a fast three-candle move (the FVG definition), or more loosely as any fast, one-directional price leg with minimal overlap. Marked as a zone and watched for retracement entries in the direction of the originating move.
failure_modes: The 'imbalance gets rebalanced' expectation fails constantly; trends leave trails of unfilled imbalances behind them, and the term is vague enough to be fitted to almost any fast move.
misconceptions: That an imbalance is a market defect the price must repair; markets have no obligation to revisit thinly traded spans, and session gaps (a different phenomenon) are often conflated with this concept.
example: During a news-driven spike, three consecutive 5-minute candles leave a 15-point span untouched between the first candle's high and the third's low — an imbalance zone marked for a possible retrace entry.

name: Premium zone
definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the upper half of a 'dealing range' — the leg between a significant swing low and swing high — i.e., everything above the 50% midpoint. The convention frames longs taken in premium as poor value and shorts in premium as acceptable value; it is a positioning heuristic, not a valuation measure.
intuition: Split the range in half; buying in the top half means paying up relative to where the market has just been.
mechanics: Anchor the dealing range at a meaningful swing low and high; the midpoint is equilibrium and the region above it is premium. SMC models look for sell-side setups (bearish order blocks, bearish FVGs) located in premium, aligned with the higher-timeframe bias.
formula: Equilibrium = (range high + range low) / 2; premium zone = prices above that midpoint within the dealing range.
failure_modes: In strong trends price lives in premium for long stretches, so 'expensive' stays expensive; the framework also depends entirely on which swing anchors are chosen.
misconceptions: That premium means overvalued in any fundamental sense; it is purely a relative position within one analyst-chosen range.
example: With a dealing range of 1800-1900, equilibrium sits at 1850; a bearish order block at 1875 lies in premium, qualifying it — under SMC convention — as a short-entry zone.

name: Discount zone
definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the lower half of a 'dealing range' — the leg between a significant swing low and swing high — i.e., everything below the 50% midpoint. The convention frames longs taken in discount as acceptable value and shorts in discount as poor value; a positioning heuristic, not a valuation measure.
intuition: Split the range in half; buying in the bottom half means paying less than the range's typical price.
mechanics: Anchor the dealing range at a meaningful swing low and high; the midpoint is equilibrium and the region below it is discount. SMC models look for buy-side setups (bullish order blocks, bullish FVGs) located in discount, aligned with the higher-timeframe bias.
formula: Equilibrium = (range high + range low) / 2; discount zone = prices below that midpoint within the dealing range.
failure_modes: In strong downtrends price keeps getting 'cheaper' without bouncing, so discount buys can average into a falling market; results hinge on discretionary anchor selection.
misconceptions: That discount means undervalued or due to rise; it only means 'below the midpoint of the chosen range', which says nothing about where price goes next.
example: With a dealing range of 1800-1900, a bullish order block at 1825 lies in discount (below the 1850 equilibrium), qualifying it — under SMC convention — as a long-entry zone.

name: Equilibrium level
aliases: consequent encroachment (when applied to a gap)
definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the 50% midpoint of a dealing range (a significant swing low to swing high), separating the premium half above from the discount half below. It serves as the reference for the methodology's value heuristic; outside SMC, a 50% midpoint is simply the midpoint of a range (also a Dow Theory retracement convention).
intuition: The range's center of gravity: above it price is relatively expensive, below it relatively cheap, within that range.
mechanics: Computed as (swing high + swing low)/2 of the chosen dealing range and drawn as a horizontal reference. SMC models use it to filter setups (longs below, shorts above) and as a mean-threshold reference on individual candles and gaps.
failure_modes: The level moves whenever the analyst re-anchors the range, so it is unstable as a signal; price shows no documented obligation to react at a range midpoint.
misconceptions: That equilibrium is a supply-demand balance price the market returns to; it is an arithmetic midpoint of an arbitrarily chosen range, not an economic equilibrium.
example: A dealing range from 1800 to 1900 puts equilibrium at 1850; price stalls near 1850 on its way from the discount half toward the range high.
